title: Cloud Computing
description: Compute, storage, networking basics across major cloud providers.

careerApplications: Nearly every backend/SWE role assumes basic comfort deploying to a cloud provider.

lessons.title: What 'the cloud' actually is
objectives: Explain cloud computing without buzzwords
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: cloud cost estimation and budgets.
Explain how cloud provider changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect cloud provider with on-demand and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: 'The cloud' is just someone else's data center, rented by the hour (or the second), accessed over the internet through an API instead of you racking physical servers. Instead of buying a machine, you request compute/storage/networking on demand from a provider (AWS, GCP, Azure), and pay only for what you use.
examples:
# Traditional: buy a server, wait weeks, run it 24/7 whether you use it or not
# Cloud: request a VM via an API call, pay per second, delete it when done
commonMistakes: Thinking 'the cloud' is one magic thing rather than a rentable version of the same servers/storage/networking you'd otherwise buy yourself.
lessons.careerRelevance: Almost no modern company racks its own physical servers anymore; this is the default deployment target. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Compute: VMs vs containers vs serverless
objectives: Contrast the three main compute options
Explain how VM changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect VM with managed containers and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A VM (virtual machine) gives you a full virtual computer you manage yourself (OS, patches, everything). A managed container service runs your Docker containers without you managing the underlying OS.
examples:
# VM: 'give me a Linux box, I'll install and manage everything'
# Container service: 'run my Docker image, I don't want to manage the OS'
# Serverless: 'run this function when a request comes in, and nothing otherwise'
commonMistakes: Choosing serverless for a workload with constant, predictable traffic — you lose the cost benefit (built for spiky/idle patterns) and pay a 'cold start' latency tax for no reason.
lessons.careerRelevance: Choosing the right compute model is a real system-design interview question.

lessons.title: Storage: object vs block vs file
objectives: Distinguish the three storage types and when each fits
Explain how object storage changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect object storage with block storage and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Object storage (like S3) stores whole files/blobs with a flat key-based lookup — great for images, backups, static assets, at massive scale, but not for a running database. Block storage is a raw disk attached to a VM (like a hard drive) — what a database needs.
examples:
# Object storage: store 10 million user-uploaded images -> S3
# Block storage: the disk backing your Postgres VM -> EBS
# File storage: a shared folder read by 5 app servers -> EFS
commonMistakes: Trying to run a database directly on object storage — it's not designed for the random, low-latency reads/writes a database needs.
lessons.careerRelevance: Picking the right storage type is a recurring system-design and cost-optimization question.

lessons.title: Networking basics (VPC, security groups)
objectives: Explain a VPC and a security group in plain terms
Explain how VPC changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect VPC with security group and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A cloud network usually lives inside a virtual private network such as a VPC. Public and private subnets separate resources that need direct internet reachability from resources that should stay behind controlled boundaries.
examples:
# security group on the database: allow inbound port 5432
# ONLY from the app server's security group -- not from 0.0.0.0/0
commonMistakes: Opening a database's port to 0.0.0.0/0 (the whole internet) 'just to get it working' — a leading cause of real data breaches.
lessons.careerRelevance: Understanding VPCs and security groups is assumed baseline knowledge for any cloud deployment task.

lessons.title: Load balancers & managed databases
objectives: Explain what a load balancer does and why managed databases exist
Explain how load balancer changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect load balancer with managed database and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: A load balancer sits in front of multiple app servers and distributes incoming traffic across them, so no single server is overwhelmed and traffic keeps flowing if one server fails. A managed database (RDS, Cloud SQL) handles backups, patching, and failover for you, so your team doesn't operate the database software itself.
examples: users -> load balancer -> [server1, server2, server3] -> managed database
commonMistakes: Running a single app server with no load balancer 'because traffic is low now' — it works until the one server needed a restart during peak hours.
lessons.careerRelevance: Load balancing and managed databases are the two most common 'first scaling step' answers in interviews.

lessons.title: Auto-scaling & designing for failure
objectives: Explain auto-scaling and why redundancy matters
Apply the KHDA-benchmarked professional additions in a realistic company workflow: cloud monitoring and utilization metrics.
Explain how auto-scaling changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect auto-scaling with redundancy and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Auto-scaling changes capacity in response to demand, but a production cloud system also needs a repeatable way to create that infrastructure.
examples:
# auto-scaling rule: if avg CPU > 70% for 5 min, add a server
# if avg CPU < 20% for 15 min, remove one
commonMistakes: Designing a system assuming the cloud provider's infrastructure never fails — availability zones exist specifically because it does, occasionally, and real architectures plan around that.
lessons.careerRelevance: Auto-scaling and fault-tolerant design are core system-design interview topics, especially for backend/AI infra roles. These additions were retained because they map to practical software/AI work rather than theory-only study.

lessons.title: Identity & Access Management (IAM)
objectives: Explain IAM's core model (principals, permissions, roles) and apply least privilege in a cloud environment
Explain how IAM changes the behavior, result, or engineering decision in a concrete example
Connect IAM with principal and predict what changes when one assumption changes
Verify the idea with a normal case and an important edge, failure, or scale case
lessons.explanation: Security groups (covered earlier) control WHAT TRAFFIC can reach a resource over the network; IAM controls WHO -- or what service -- is allowed to perform WHICH ACTIONS on your cloud resources, regardless of network access.
commonMistakes: Granting a service or user broad admin-level permissions because it's faster than scoping a precise policy -- this turns any single leaked credential or buggy script into a much larger blast.
lessons.careerRelevance: IAM misconfigurations (overly broad permissions, unused old credentials) are a leading real-world cause of cloud security incidents -- least-privilege thinking is expected baseline knowledge for anyone operating real cloud infrastructure.

exercises.title: Diagnose an over-permissioned service
exercises.prompt: A backend service that only needs to read from one specific storage bucket is currently running with a full-admin IAM role, because it was faster to set up. The security group is correctly locked down. Is this actually secure? What's the real risk, and what's the fix?
exercises.hint: no -- a correctly locked-down security group only controls network access, not what the service is ALLOWED to do once it's running; the fix is scoping the IAM policy to exactly the permission needed (e.g. read access to that one bucket), so a bug or leaked credential can't be used to do anything beyond that

interviewPreparation.q: What's the difference between what a security group controls and what IAM controls?
interviewPreparation.a: A security group is network-level -- it controls what traffic can even reach a resource. IAM is action-level -- it controls what a principal (user, service, role) is allowed to DO once it has access, regardless of the network path. A service can have a perfectly locked-down security group and still be a major security risk if its IAM permissions are far broader than it actually needs.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you decide between a VM, a managed container service, and serverless for a given workload?
interviewPreparation.a: Serverless fits spiky, infrequent, short-lived workloads well since you pay only for actual execution time, but has cold-start latency and execution time limits. Managed containers fit steady, longer-running services well. A raw VM makes sense when you need full control over the environment that a managed service doesn't give you. The deciding factors are traffic pattern, acceptable latency, and how much operational control you actually need.

interviewPreparation.q: What does 'designing for failure' actually mean in a cloud architecture?
interviewPreparation.a: Assuming any single component -- a VM, an availability zone, even a whole region -- can fail at any time, and architecting so the system survives it: redundancy across availability zones, auto-scaling to replace failed instances, load balancers routing around unhealthy nodes. It's a mindset shift from 'prevent failure' to 'assume failure and survive it.'

interviewPreparation.q: Why is the principle of least privilege important in cloud IAM specifically?
interviewPreparation.a: Cloud credentials and roles are attached to automated services, not just humans, and a single leaked key or a bug in automated code can be exploited immediately at scale. Scoping permissions to exactly what's needed limits the blast radius of any single compromised credential or buggy deployment, rather than one mistake having full account-wide consequences.

interviewPreparation.q: How would you design an auto-scaling policy for a web application, and what could go wrong with a poorly chosen one?
interviewPreparation.a: Pick a metric that actually reflects load (CPU, request count, queue depth) and thresholds with enough margin to react before users are affected, plus a reasonable cooldown so it doesn't thrash. A poorly chosen policy either scales too slowly (users see degraded performance before new capacity arrives) or too aggressively (rapid scale up/down cycles that waste cost and can even destabilize the service).

capstone.title: Deploy and operate your system in a real cloud environment
capstone.description: Take the containerized system you've already built (from the Docker capstone, or a new one) and actually run it in a cloud environment -- not just containerized locally, but deployed to a managed service with real cloud infrastructure around it: a load balancer, a managed database, auto-scaling, and IAM permissions scoped to least privilege. This capstone answers a genuinely different question than Docker's: not 'can you package this,' but 'can you deploy and operate this in an environment designed for real traffic and real failure.'
deliverables: The service deployed to a managed cloud compute service (not just running Docker locally) with a real, reachable URL
A managed database and/or load balancer in front of the service, not a single unmanaged instance
An auto-scaling policy with a stated metric and thresholds, plus a written justification for why those thresholds make sense for this workload
IAM permissions scoped to least privilege for anything the service accesses (storage, database) -- no broad admin credentials
A short architecture diagram plus a written note on one specific failure mode you designed for (an availability zone going down, a traffic spike, a dependency becoming unavailable)
capstone.portfolioTips: The failure-mode write-up is what separates this from 'I clicked deploy' -- naming a specific failure you designed for, and how your architecture actually handles it, is exactly the kind of reasoning a cloud/infrastructure interview probes for.

industryUsage.usage: Runs almost entirely on cloud infrastructure (AWS) and is widely cited for designing explicitly around failure -- assuming any given component, zone, or region can fail at any time, and architecting to survive it.
As both a cloud provider and a massive cloud customer internally, treats auto-scaling and IAM least-privilege as baseline operational practice across its own services, not optional hardening.

Operates at a scale where cloud architecture decisions (managed databases, load balancing, auto-scaling policies) directly affect both reliability and infrastructure cost, making these skills a real, practical requirement rather than theoretical.
